utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I was informed, Mr. Kehoe, that you would like to address the Court on a certain matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour two brief issues. The first one comes from the summaries I noticed in the filing that the Prosecution made on the summary of the witness's testimony. On three separate occasions in that summary it is noted that the witness saw dead civilians. If you examine the actual witness statement, he says civilians and soldiers on those three occasions. Of course, that is admitting from the summary so I asked my colleague across the well if in fact in his summary to the public it would include civilians and soldiers and of course it doesn't. It just notes civilians. I'm not sure of what exact purpose of those summaries are, if it's a Prosecutor's version of the facts or an objective assessment of what is in the witness's statements. I don't know if you want to address -- me to move to the next issue, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The statement actually in --the witness's statement actually says that he saw dead civilians, although some were in uniform. He doesn't identify specifically soldiers. He does say that he saw some of the dead civilians that he saw lying in the streets were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I don't see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if what is an issue it -- of course, it's a summary but if you then add the three, four, or five words that Mr. Kehoe considers to be relevant it is not evidence. I mean, the original is evidence, if it would meet the concerns of Mr. Kehoe is there any reason not to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next issue is to do with the actual statement itself, and it goes to the page 7 opinion rendered by Colonel Bellerose and I'm talking about page seven, the first full paragraph after -- the first paragraph to the carry-over paragraph where he gives his opinion the shelling was carried out to drive the civilian population away from Knin because the shelling was not directed at specific military targets. Of course that, is an opinion. I tried at that talk to my colleague across the we well, Mr. Russo, to eliminate that and limit it to just what Colonel Bellerose saw, what he observed during the operative time-frame. Mr. Russo declined to take that invitation. I will say if that testimony is led during the course of direct examination it will of course compel the Defence to go through the military target exercise and the lack of knowledge that this witness had concerned the military targets in the Knin area. Frankly, Judge, I know you have called upon us to shorten things and I attempted to do that in this fashion, but I will say that if that goes forward in that fashion I will be forced to meet it in defence of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This is certainly an issue that has come up in the past. I think we have handled it in correctly in the past. The Court has been quite clear that these opinions standing alone don't count for much. Of course, the factual basis underlying the opinion, something that would assist the Court in determining what led the witness to come to this assessment, I certainly intend to explore the factual basis underlying that opinion. We have provided that to the Defence in a supplemental information sheet indicating why the witness came to that opinion. I think it's something that will assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I -- then of course you're fully entitled to explore the matter in cross-examination. I do not really see the procedural issue, apart from, of course the Chamber would never expect a part to give up an important matter just for sake of time. That may be clear to everyone. And, as Mr. Russo rightly said, or should I said rightly understood, that standing alone of course to say this was not against military targets without laying a proper factual foundation, it might be one of the core issues in this case. So, therefore, it certainly needs a factual basis and if it is there, then of course it is there to be challenged as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand. I just want to highlight it before I moved into the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Another matter, of course, is how efficient that is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, that is a double-edged sword because if efficiency calls for us to meet that, which I will do, that is going take some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But even then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't have to discuss it any further, I think. It is clear that it will take sometime. It may also be clear that the more efficient way it is done, the less extra time it takes. Mr. Russo, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Joseph Lorenzo Claude Bellerose, witness 97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from the matters just dealt with, which are not considered to be objections against admission of the 92 ter statement as such, apart from this -- this opinion matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there is no objection from any of the Defence teams. That's then clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bellerose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bellerose, before you give evidence in this court the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speaks the truth the whole truth and nothing butt truth. The text is now handed out to you but Madam Usher and I would like to invite to you make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Bellerose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by Mr. Russo, who is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bellerose.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me first apologise on behalf of our office for having kept you here for so long waiting. Thank you for your patience and I would ask you please to state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Joseph Lorenzo Claude Bellerose.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And Mr. Bellerose, do you recall giving two statements to the ICTY, one dated 1st November 1995, the other dated that 2nd of November 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5205.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Prosecution counsel is kindly requested to speak into the microphone or maybe even into another microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you got the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to speak into the microphone or in another microphone. The microphone you're using at this time is relatively far away and perhaps obstructed a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I apologise Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Bellerose, do you see your statement there on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It's coming up in just a second.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise that as your 1 November 1995 statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Is it possible to scroll -- scroll through, to the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bellerose, you mean page by page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes, it's yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Registrar, if we could now have 65 ter 5232. And if we could scroll to the last signature page. Mr. Bellerose, do you recognise that as your 2 November 1995 -- 1999 statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review both of those statements before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are those statements true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, they are true and accurate to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do both of those statements correctly reflect the information that you gave ICTY investigators.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you were examined with regard to those same matters here today, would your answers be the same as in those statements?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would move for the admission of 65 ter 5205, 65 ter 5232.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I established before, there are no objections against admission. Mr. Registrar, first the November 1995 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P545.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P545 is admitted into evidence. Then the November 1999 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P546, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P546 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could please have the assistance of the court usher I would like to give the witness hard copies of his statements. And with your permission, Mr. President I would like to read a brief summary of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. "Mr. Bellerose was the sector engineer for the whole of Sector South from 15 June until 16 December 1995 and was responsible for supervising all engineering work, including construction of observation posts and demining. In connection with his duties he travelled extensively throughout Sector South both prior to and after Operation Storm. He observed that there were not many soldiers in Knin prior to Operation Storm, and even in his travels throughout the sector, he only saw small groups of four or five ARSK soldiers at a time. He was present in Knin during the artillery attack on the 4th and 5th of August, 1995, and observed the shelling from the balcony of the UN HQ building. "Mr. Bellerose delivered medical supplies to the hospital during the shelling on the 4th of August and observed a great deal of devastation, including dead civilians an individuals in uniform lying in the streets, injured people at the hospital with limbs missing and buildings and cars on fire. "While he was supervising the delivery of medical supplies at the hospital, shells were flying over his head and impacting in the town. He proposed and implemented the plan for accommodating the Serbs who sought refuge in the UN HQ compound, most of whom were women, children and the elderly. "After Operation Storm, on 6 August, he observed Croatian authorities bringing in civilian trucks to clean up the main road in Knin. On 9 August he travelled to the water-pumping station for Knin to try and restore water service and observed that almost every house and apartment in Knin had been looted. During his travels throughout the sector after Operation Storm, he observed that many villages were deployed by burning and looting. He was often prevented from entering villages by Croatian special police and would later see smoke rising from houses in those villages." Your Honour, that concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Bellerose, I would first like to discuss the situation in Sector South prior to Operation Storm. Can you please give the Court some idea for how extensively you travelled in the sector prior to the artillery attack?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to the attack, one of my main role was to oversee the reinforcement of all the UN observation posts. As such, I believe there was 120 observation posts between the Serb and the Croat border, and I visited each one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And during these trips did you ever have occasion to see any ARSK observation posts?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I saw a few observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you please give the Court an idea for the state of those observation posts?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: The observation posts that I saw, they were called very substandard, affording very little overhead protection in case of artillery or direct fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you give the Court some idea of how equipped or manned these observation posts were?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: At the observation posts that I saw, I didn't see any heavy equipment or artillery pieces. Basically the observation posts were manned by two, three, four, maybe five ARSK soldier, at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And during these trips to all of the observation posts, did you have the opportunity to observe the living conditions in the Republic of Serbian Krajina generally?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: We're talking about civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: There was a big difference into the standard of living of the people in Croatia into the Serb area. For me, looking back, in the Serb area, it's like I was going into a third world country where there was not many vehicle moving around. Most people were walking or having horse or donkey pulling carts. It was very poor standard of living.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now move to the events of -- in Knin on 4 August 1995. Can you please tell the Court what you observed, what you saw and heard of the shelling on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: The shelling started, I believe, around 5.00 in the morning on the 4th, and it was very intensive for about a period of one to two hours. From the sound, it sounded like the artillery was all over the place, in -- you know, and there was no really any specific target. Then after an hour or two, it slowed down. And then you could hear artillery landing everywhere in town, in -- you know, until I got on to the balcony of the UN headquarters then I could see that they were landing in the different parts of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could direct you to your second statement, that is P546, and page 3 of your second statement, the fourth paragraph. And in the B/C/S translation that's page 3, second paragraph. And there you reference that the initial shelling began at 5.00 a.m., and you state: "I could tell by the noise that some shelling was artillery fire and some was rocket fire." Could you please explain to the Court how you were able to distinguish that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: At the time I believe there was, because of my military training, where I had previously seen a rocket fired during a fire-power demonstration.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And staying again in that same paragraph, you indicate that you went to the top floor of the UN HQ building to observe the shelling and that you saw shells landing in the railway goods yard near the northern barracks and you also saw them exploding in Knin close to the hill where the winding road from Gracac passes. Can you please clarify for the Court whether these are the only areas in which you saw shells landing in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, it was not the only places. Those are the ones that stuck to my mind that I could locate or be able to identify on a map or photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving to your first statement, that's P545, it's that one-page, at paragraph 1 - it's the same in the B/C/S - you indicate that you took a trip to Knin hospital to deliver medical supplies on the 4th, sometime between 1600 and 1800 hours. I would like you to please describe that trip for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I was asked by the Chief of Staff, General Leslie, to go to the hospital -- well, the purpose of the trip was two -- threefold. First we had to take General Forand to the Serb headquarters. Also to go to the hospital to deliver medical supply. And on our way back our task was to go to several houses that we knew were UN civilian employee or -- and UN civilian police were residing and to bring them back to safety inside the UN camp. We did the trip with two armoured person carrier, one M-113 and one OT-64. Inside the trip I was inside the vehicle, so I could not see what was happening, but I could hear artillery shell landing. When we got to the hospital, I got out of the vehicle and supervised the unloading of medical supply. While I was outside the hospital and outside the armoured personnel carrier, I could hear shell flying overhead and hearing them explode inside Knin. On our way back I was inside the armoured personnel carrier and then when we got the location of the address where we knew civilian police, UN civilian police and UN employees were living, then I got outside the vehicle and I could see devastation in the street. Some bodies were lying down, some cars were on fire, and I could hear artillery round impacting to the town. Once we pick up as many people as we could and retrieve General Forand, we went back to the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Let me ask you, Mr. Bellerose, while you were at the hospital, did you see an ARSK tank anywhere in the area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you see any evidence that a tank or multiple tanks had been stationed near the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let's please move back it your second statement, that is P546, at page 4, in the third paragraph. And in the B/C/S translation that would be page 4 at the top of the page. And there you discuss the same trip but in more detail, and you indicate that: "Driving through Knin on this mission I saw a great deal of devastation. There were a number of what appeared to be dead civilians lying in the streets, although some were in uniform. Buildings and cars were on fire and there was devastation everywhere I looked." I think you have explained to the Court that you made these observations while you were outside the APC. Let me ask you during your proofing session did you have a chance to mark on an aerial photograph of Knin some of the locations where you stopped as well as where you saw the shells impacting in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5303. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Bellerose, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are you able to describe for the Court the markings that you made?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Court what the circle towards the bottom labelled A represents?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Represent two things. The first is -- this is where I saw three artillery round, as per my first statement, landing and it also represent one of the area where we stop to pick up some UN employees, civilian employee, and UN civilian police. So we had several stop in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the circle directly above that which is labelled C?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: This is where I saw one artillery round landing at the north railway tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the circle above and to the left of that, which is marked D?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: D, this is another area we stop on the way back from the hospital to pick up UN and civilian and UN police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And, finally, the circle far to the left which is marked B?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: That's where my first statement I identify one artillery round landing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move for the admission of 65 ter 5305.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P547.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P547 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Moving now to the 5th of August, 1995, Mr. Bellerose, can you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, would you allow me one question. In the witness statement we see what appears to be civilians although in uniforms. How do you identify someone in a uniform as being a civilian? Could you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo just read part of your statement and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the Court's benefit that is second statement, page 4, third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- Mr. Russo read to you from your statement, saying: "There were a number of what appeared to be dead civilians lying in the streets, although some were in uniform." Could you tell us exactly how you identify a dead person in uniform being a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe at the time what I meant to say was that there was some dead civilian and also there was some dead people in uniform, meaning the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you therefore do not express any opinion about whether those persons in uniform were civilians or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't mean to say that those person in uniform were civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Bellerose, if you could please explain to the Court the observations you made regarding the shelling that occurred on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: The shelling on the 5th of August was, when it started in the morning was still very extensive for the first hour. I believe it started near 0515 hours. And then later on, during the day, it was of not extensive at all. There was very sporadic, one shell maybe every ten, 15 minutes, and there were at all -- all over the place. There was not one specific location. That was later on that during the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bellerose, can you tell the Court whether, on either the 4th or the 5th of August, if you ever saw or heard any outgoing artillery fire from Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I never saw nor did I hear any outgoing fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could move to your second statement again. That's P546. At page 7. This is in the B/C/S, page 6. At the last full paragraph you offer some opinions and I will quote: "In my opinion the shelling of Knin was carried out to drive away of the civilian population. The shelling was not directed at specific military targets. I believe it was deliberate harassment shelling." Now I would like to discuss the factual basis for each one of these opinions separately. First let me ask you, what was the basis for your opinion that the shelling was carried out to drive away the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: In my opinion, if there would have been military target in those location that would have been causing a threat to the Croat forces, they would have been more intensive and direct at a specific target, be more concentrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what you observed that was not consistent with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: The artillery fire wasn't concentrated into one location. It was landing all over the town more to a random fashion and at random interval.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And you indicated that the shelling was not directed at specific military targets. Let me ask you first to please identify or tell the Court what you believed the military targets to be at the time and why.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: For what I have seen in my time in Knin, the military target would have been the north camp, the camp adjacent to the UN compound and the RSK headquarter in downtown Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. You also offered the opinion that it was deliberate harassment fire, and I would like you to please explain for the Court what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Because it was like a random firing all over the place and random interval, you know, for me, I believed that this is -- this is a situation that will make the occupants of the town, if they were still there, wondering if they were going to be next or when the next round was going to land, if it would be close to their place. Just that, I don't know, it's hard for me to explain, but it wasn't -- makes you wonder if the next round is going to be in your backyard as opposed to, you know, five -- 500 metres or, you know, five miles down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the military targets that you identified, the north camp, the camp adjacent to the UN compound and the RSK headquarters in downtown Knin, can you tell the Court whether from your observations you saw fire being concentrated on those areas?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like you to explain for the Court if during the times that you observed the shelling of Knin, if you saw artillery fire being concentrated on either what you identify as the north camp or the RSK headquarters or the Serb camp next to the UN base.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move now to some of the events that followed Operation Storm and if we could move to page 5 of your second statement at the fourth paragraph in the very middle of the page and in the B/C/S translation this is at page 4. It's the last full paragraph. And in there, Mr. Bellerose, you state that: "On the 6th of August you saw that the Croats were bringing in civilian trucks to clean up the main road through Knin." I'd like you to explain to the Court what exactly it was that you observed which led you to conclude that the purpose of these trucks was to clean up the main road.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I've been in the construction business as an engineer for most of my life, and that morning of the 6th what I saw going to Knin were basically construction truck. There were like contractors truck that carried construction material, plywood, two by four, window replacement glass, and there was several one of them, so like the type of trucks that you see going to a major construction site and also the material that it was carrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And in that same paragraph -- I'm sorry, on the same page in the next paragraph you describe a trip that you took on the 9th of August to try and restore water service to the UN camp and this appears in the B/C/S translation at the top of the page 5. Let me ask you, Mr. Bellerose, do you know why was no water supply in the compound at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: The pumping station was no longer working and also some of the water line had been broken because of artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. In that same paragraph describing the trip that you took into the town on that day, you indicated and I will quote: "There was devastation everywhere in Knin. It was obvious that looting had taken place. There was clothing and other items lying beneath the windows of almost every house and apartment." And I would like to ask you, did the devastation that you witnessed on that day include damage from shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And based on what you observed, was this damage from shelling concentrated in any particular area of the town?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. It was all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And moving to the last paragraph at the bottom of page 5 of your second statement. In the B/C/S this is page 5, the third paragraph. You mention an incident on the 12th of August where you discovered the body of an ARSK soldier who had been shot in the chest and you offer your opinion that he had been executed, and I would like you to please explain for the Court what it was about the circumstances that led to you form that opinion.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yeah, for me, the body was just lying down on a straight fashion, just like if the person had been lying down on his back and, you know, had been shot. I'm no expert on crime scene investigation, but, for me, if somebody would have been standing up and shot in the back when they are falling down, his body would have probably been arm twisted, leg -- you know, but it wouldn't be straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And turning to page 6of your second statement, the top paragraph, and in the B/C/S this is page 5, the fourth paragraph, you indicate that after Operation Storm the Croatian special police often stopped you from entering some villages and that you would later see houses in those villages on fire. I would like you to please explain for the Court these kinds of incidents, how did they happen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: At that time we had been directed by General Forand to start dismantling all the observation posts and return them to the -- the ground in pristine condition. One of my tasks was go and oversee all the dismantle of the OPs and travelling throughout the sector, several times, you know, we get to a village trying to go to that village to get to an observation and the special police were blocking the roads and telling us it wasn't safe to go through the area because they were conducting operation. And so we -- we went and tried to get to another OP and quite often on the way back we could see that one or two houses in that village had been set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. You described these soldiers as Croatian special police. Can you describe for the Court what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: They were wearing one or two-piece uniform that was either, going from memory, either dark grey or black. They also were wearing black load bearing vest, a vest that where you could put ammunition, carry your ammunition or grenades. They looked very professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the incidents that you described where they prevented you from entering villages that you later saw houses burning in, could you give the Court some idea of how often this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Maybe three or four times. It's hard for me to recall right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are you able to tell the Court in what area generally any of these incidents occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I remember once or twice going toward Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And also in that same paragraph you state: "The Croats allowed us to use the main roads but kept us away from villages on the side roads." Can you please explain for the Court how exactly you were kept on the main roads?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: They had roadblocks with check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court who was manning those check-points?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: The special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bellerose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. I have one matter which I would like to seek clarification of. Mr. Bellerose, Mr. Russo invited you to explain to us what it was that you observed which led you to conclude that the purpose of these trucks was to clean up the main road, and then your answer was about what they were carrying and what your experience as an engineer told you about that, plywood, two by four, window replacement glass. Now, if I look at your statement, I see that the portion read to you by Mr. Russo is part of a sentence which is "they were tidying up the main street for the benefit of the media. That is my considered belief." That follows the sentence which said "they were bringing in civilian trucks to clean up the main road through Knin." Apparently there are two issues in your statement. One is cleaning up the main road through Knin and the other one is tidying up the main street for the benefit of the media. The question put to you about the trucks was focussing at to clean the main road. Your answer seemed to be rather reconstruction. At least I have some difficulties in understanding what you exactly said, also because you said it was for the benefit of the media. Could you elaborate on the matters that are still puzzling me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- when I first went into Knin after the offensive -- well, let's go back. When I went in town, on the main street and when we pick up General Forand, there was devastation. Window glass on that street were broken and there was a lot of devastation in town. When we went back out to go to the water station that Wednesday, the main street had been cleaned up. Now, yes, we could see devastation throughout Knin, that sign of looting, but that main street in front of the ARSK headquarters had been cleaned up. Window had -- glasses had been replaced, and you know, it was obvious that there was some tidying up that had been happening on that street. And also -- I mean, that's -- also it's an opinion that, you know, for me, there was -- it was a public relation because the press, when they started to come to our camp to try to interview us, I recall somebody from -- you know, telling me that they been restricted to basically some of the main street of Knin. So this is where I probably derived that statement from, that that was for the purpose of the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I have to understand that what you saw you considered to be an organised attempt to make things look better than actually they were. Is that, in short what you were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm trying to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bellerose, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe, who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. How are you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, just turning to your statement, your first -- your second statement, and that would be P546. I believe you have it in front of you. And you note in the first page of that document -- actually, it is the second page, last paragraph that when you -- "I arrived Knin in the middle of June 1995, I could feel a tension in the area. I believe that everyone knew that something was going to take place." Do you see that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, during this time were you aware of military activities by the HV in the Livno valley?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Can you refresh my memory? Where is the Livno valley --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the other side of the Dinara.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: So that would be east of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Actually, that would be west of Sector South. If you're looking out the front, it would be west.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, you do, okay. Now -- I do apologise, that is east. As you look to the right that is east you're absolutely right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, whatever direction you look, things are always east or west from other point, or north or south, but it doesn't change if we look at it from a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's true, it was east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, it was east.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you were aware of that, were you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And during this time when you got here there was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. Mr. Bellerose, you quickly moved from east to west. That's not what you're supposed to do if it really is east.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I understand. But I didn't recall the Livno valley afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. But the last --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- last words of Mr. Kehoe were "it would it be would be west," and then you said "yes, I do recall." That is at least ambiguous. Could you try to focus very much on what is said and what your answer is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And my apologies, Colonel, I mean I was the confusing party here, Your Honour, and I do apologise to the Court, to the witness, and the Livno valley is in fact east. Now, the tension did include hijackings by the RSK, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were forced to travel in pairs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: That was hijacking a vehicle and not personnel, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Hijacking of vehicles but you were forced to travel in pairs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I may and if I can turn to your diary, which is 65 ter 5285.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Can I see a copy of the diary? I don't have it in front of me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did bring a hard copy for the witness in case this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I take it that there is no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Quite all right, quite all right. Colonel, absolutely. And frankly, I apologise for not having it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist Mr. Russo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning your attention to the 28th of July, 1995, and that would be at page -- if we're looking at the top of that document it is 06354619. At the bottom of the page. If we can page up till 28th of July using the -- let's just go to the bottom of that page. 28th of July, notes "interesting day. HV, HVO, Croatians took the town of Bosansko Grahovo in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This cut one of the Serbs' main supply routes. General mobilisation is happening in town." Now taking that general mobilisation happening in town, I'd like to read a piece of testimony from a Prosecution witness a UN CIVPOL representative Jan Elleby. And he noted at page 3474, line 6: "Now as we move through July of 1995, you note in your supplemental information sheet -- well, I actually think it begins on P214 -- that you saw a lot of soldiers in the street. In your supplemental sheet you note that you observed an increased number of RSK troops in Knin in this period. In the period building up to the beginning of Operation Storm can you tell us about that a little bit." "Answer: Yes, the assessment of the picture in the streets in the town was that from a few days in July and up to the end of July there came more and more military vehicles, more and more uniformed military personnel." "Question: And did you and our CIVPOL monitors observe that while you were driving around the area. "Answer is: Yes." Now, you know note there was a general mobilisation in town and Mr. Elleby notes that will more and more uniformed personnel. Is Mr. Elleby's observations consistent with your own and do they likewise reflect your statement in your diary that a general mobilisation is happening in town?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: If we go to my statement in my diary, I believe that the statement came from information that was passed at one of the staff meeting at the sector headquarters. For me, on the day leading to 4th and 5th of August, during that period, I was very busy visiting every observation post, so I used to leave Knin quite earlier in the morning to be at the various observation posts. So quite often, when I was leaving the town, I didn't see too many people on the street, and when I was driving through the sector, I didn't see. So, I cannot comment on -- on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when you -- and I'm just waiting for the translation to catch up, Colonel. When the issue of general mobilisation came to your attention at Sector South headquarters, what did these other individuals say that the ARSK was doing to mobilise?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the town of -- of Knin itself. While you were driving in there did you observe men wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the people that were in camouflage uniforms, did you note that they were in a large age category from young men to older men?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware that ARSK had arms depots around Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Before I went -- or before the 4th and 5th, I was unaware. I was made aware of one of them afterwards, near Strmica, or on the road between the water station and Strmica. I could not locate it on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you were never there yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I was there, but it was afterwards when everything had been removed from the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, likewise during this period of time if we can turn to your diary at 06354598, the ARSK was restricting your movement, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the top of the page on 06354598, the entry for June 22nd. It should be paragraph 3 for June 22nd. You see that second sentence: "I don't know why, but sometimes they restrict our movement."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: It did happen on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the ARSK was preventing you from going to certain locations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, can I remember twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what locations were they?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note in your diary, as we read previously, that Bosansko Grahovo fell towards the latter part of July. Were you aware that after that the ARSK was planning a counterattack against the HV to retake Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just by way of background you knew the importance of Knin to the RSK, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Not really. Well, other than being the former capital of the Krajina, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And was it considered in your conversations with your colleagues and anybody else in the area, was Knin considered to be the centre of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't remember discussing this or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, what I'd like to do at this point is touch on a few topics that are referred in your statement and that were also referred to by Mr. Russo. So to the extent that we're jumping around a little bit --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No. Also, maybe I would like to clarify to the Court, I know Mr. Kehoe, you're referring to me as a Colonel but I did retire as a lieutenant-colonel, so I'm retired right now, so I just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge. It's a habit out of respect and as long as -- if you're uncomfortable with it, I'll call you Mr. Bellerose.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I don't have a problem, it's just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. Now, you noted during the course of your direct testimony about observation posts, and you talked about some of these observations posts being poorly constructed and we're going to get to that in a second? I would first, with regard to the weaponry involved, you did see the ARSK with heavy weaponry while you were in the area, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: During the period that I was there what I saw was some -- few artillery piece, some D-20 being towed. I saw one D 34/85 with a -- missing a cannon where the cannon was broken and I saw a couple of BMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what is a BMP?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is the last one?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: BMP, it Russian-made armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk about that for a second and talk about the D-20s that is in fact in your diary. At June the 20th, page 06354595 towards the bottom. Paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "On the way to JorBat we saw six artillery pieces being towed. They were IDd as ID-20s. They were going towards Benkovac." I would like to pull up on the screen, and I think we have to do this via Sanction, Your Honour. I stand corrected. It is now in e-court and it is 1D36-0008. These are two pages, Colonel, from a UN recognition handbook of the former Yugoslavia, if you can just scroll that page a little bit, that is issued -- had been issued by the national defence. And if we could then turn to the next page. Colonel, that is a D 20 Howitzer, a 152 millimetre with an effective rage of 17.3 kilometres. You saw six of those being towed by the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll offer into evidence 1D36-0008.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D512, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D512 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, you said in your diary that these were headed towards Benkovac. Do you know in fact where they went?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I don't. No, I don't remember where they went. We radioed in and hoping that UNMO were going to follow up on the lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this weapon, this D 20, it notes it goes into a Howitzer category, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just staying, if we will, for the co -- this OPs, the observation posts that were looking at and examining and you tell us in your statement that General Forand had you looking at these various observation posts. And let me just turn your attention to your diary again, 65 ter 5282 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time if I could just offer into evidence the diary 65 ter 5285.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D513, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that then the whole of the diary --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you're speaking to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's not that long, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D513 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if we can move to your entry of the 12th of July on 06354612, paragraph 1. That's towards the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I'm just waiting for it to come up on the screen, Colonel, so others can view it. At the bottom it says: "Today the commander Brigadier-General Forand had a conference with all the battalion commanders to discuss op or 0795 SCR 981 and he -- his proposal option 1 and 2, "I was present and everybody doesn't agree with the sector commander, the orders do not make sense." What is that order, sir, the SCR 981?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention just briefly to D288, which is the order for active presence. If we can turn to the next page. Colonel, this is an order written by General Al Rodan on the 24th of July 1995 and you can see at paragraph D it has the SCR 981, 95. Were you familiar with this order for active presence?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I have to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please do, just have a quick look at it.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Is it possible to zoom a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing that document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Well, the meeting that you had we just had from the diary was on the 12th, and you noted in your statement, and I'm talking about page -- statements page 2 and 3 and that would be -- page -- P546, I believe. Yes, P546. Two and three in the English. Talking about the observation posts towards the bottom: "These Serb OPs are overlooking the Zone of Separation and were sometimes built close to the UN observation posts. Several were built very close to CanBat OPs and the Brigadier-General ordered that the Kenyans make the Serbs move their OPs and as a result of this, some of the Serb OPs were moved and others were not." So during this period of time there was a series co-location problem where the ARSK forces were in the same location of the UN observation posts. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: In the Kenyan sector, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you noted that -- well, let me turn to your diary very quickly -- well, before I get into it just in the Kenyan section, weren't there co-location problems in the CanBat areas and near Obrovac and Rastovac and Petrum [phoen] and Priste [phoen], weren't there co-location problems in those locales as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I remember one in the Canadian and that was on I believe the big mountain called Petrum, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't recall any of the others?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you visited them all?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So did you visit them starting in June and up till Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it is possible that the co-location problem came in -- became a problem after you visited that observation post?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct. Especially -- well, in the Canadian sector their OP were in very good condition so when General Forand asked us to reinforce the observation post, I concentrate into the Canadian and the Jordanian OP -- the Kenyan and Jordanian. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now these observation posts where there was co-location was readily observable, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what was -- what was the reaction of the HV when they observed the UN observation posts and the ARSK observation posts co-located?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ask?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ask anybody?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned to us that some of the ARSK observation posts were not of a higher quality. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And would they have been in the CanBat area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: The one that I saw on mount Prism [phoen] was dug in, had fairly good protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I -- I -- I apologise there. I think I came across as CanBat. I'm talking about KenBat.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Oh, Ken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Was one of the areas that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we in order to avoid any confusion and also to make the work of the transcribers possible make a distinction between Canadian and Kenyan clearly and not just by referring to them as can -- whether it is pronounced as can or ken. It goes beyond my --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Beyond ken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do apologise, because part is my pronunciation as well, apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Kenyan battalion. Was one of the locations that you noted as being substandard in the Kenyan battalion area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, both the Kenyan and the Serb OP were very substandard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to your diary on the 13th of July, that's page 06354614, the day after your meeting with General Forand. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It notes: "With CO Kenyan bat, KenBat, to do a requi for his new HQ. We found a place presently occupied by the Serbs. We can have the site provided we gave them 5.000 litres of diesel and 200 litres of petrol. Chief of Staff -- " that would be Colonel Leslie, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: " -- agreed to 500 litres and 100 litres. Sector commander was not informed and will be kept in the dark. Only a few people will know about the deal." Now, first part of this, Colonel, is that you wanted a location for the Kenyan battalion that was being occupied by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct. What was happening was the Kenyan battalion headquarters was located really close to the Canadian -- to the Canadian sector. And the idea was to relocate that headquarters so it would be more centralised within their own area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My point is that there was a location that was being occupied by the Serbs that the UN wanted.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And they wanted it so much, they were willing to pay the Serbs for that location.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: The problem at that site is there was some Serb vehicle, some trucks, and it -- in order for those truck to be moved, they needed fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yeah. My question was, in order to get that particular location, you were willing to pay the Serbs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in order to move the Serb trucks, you didn't need 500 litres of diesel and a 100 litres of petrol, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you needed that, why didn't you tell General Forand?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I reported to the Chief of Staff. I don't know why General Leslie didn't want to talk to General Forand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it was General Leslie's decision to keep this information away from General Forand?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, what -- have you concluded what the reaction of the HV was when they found out that the UN was selling petrol to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Can you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Perhaps there could be some foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Selling petrol to the Serbs. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you learn, Colonel, that the HV found out that the UN was selling diesel fuel and petrol to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but I'm not sure where the selling of the petrol to the Serbs is coming from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not make it too much of a semantic discussion where under commercial law it would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Bartering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- completed -- well, at least one -- apparently what happened at least from what I understand until now is that 500 litres of diesel are given in return to allowing the UN forces to have a certain position. Whether you would call that selling or not is not, I think, the major issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, there is foundation for this in Mr. Hill's testimony which was confirmed by General Forand that approximately a million litres of fuel was going missing a month and General Forand did confirm that it was being black marketed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, black marketed. But I have not yet hear -- whether this is black market or not is still to be seen or whether it is a fair compensation for some disadvantage. You could give it a lot of names. At this movement what apparently stands is that 500 litres, although 5.000 were asked, were given in return --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 1.000 were asked, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1.000. Oh, then I had difficulties in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think it says 1.000 litres of diesel and 2.000 litres of petrol. I said five. It should be one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, in the original the handwriting it -- we could even ask the witness because he is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ask the witness, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did -- what was asked, 5.000 or a thousand litres, I think, so apart from the 200 litres of petrol, what was the initial request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was one thousand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One thousand, yes. Is a bit unclear in writing. But that is clarified. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, continuing on, staying in your diary there Colonel, it says: "Only a few people will know about this deal." Who knew about it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: General Leslie, myself, and I'm not quite sure about who would have been the other person. Probably -- if I was to speculate, probably somebody into the logistics section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the logistics section?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Well, somebody would have to account for the fuel, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who would that be?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Captain Berikoff know about this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, let me ask you, what -- you said that you didn't know if the HV found out about this. What would you expect the HV reaction to be if they became aware of this transaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't see the relevance of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from that, it calls for speculation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you would agree, Colonel, that over time, a degree of suspicion and -- there was -- let me withdraw that. You would agree that certainly after Operation Storm there was an uncomfortable arrangement between the HV and the UN Sector South as to how the relationship was going to proceed. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I had very, very little dealing with HV troops after Operation Storm. For me, I had maybe one or two meeting with them, trying to found out the location of their minefield. Most of the dealing with the HV was done, I believe, with lieutenant-colonel Tymchuk, which was the Senior Liaison Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you were aware that the HV viewed the UN with suspicion, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And part of that suspicion -- let's put aside what happened with the OPs and the fuel. Part of that suspicion came with how the UN dealt with the Serbs that were in the UN Sector South camp after August the 4th, 1995. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to go into this at some length. I don't know if Your Honour wants to break now or I can keep going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think to have the break now would be better. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have been informed about an issue regarding the address of the witness in the witness statements. At this point I would ask for them to be temporarily admitted under seal. I will have redacted versions uploaded so that his full address is not viewable if that's all right with the Defense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, block all of it out, all the personal information out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this a general offer, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just Judge, look, I've been around this for a while. It's a general offer if you're talking about -- not the whole thing but you know, the personal information, the Colonel's address, et cetera, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, for the time being, the witness statements will be under seal, because the address of the witness appears. Then we will have a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the parties' information, I will put a request to the court management services to see whether there is any possibility to get the clock in my room at a different time than 12 minutes before 11.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, just being go back, I noted for you that at line -- I believe it is line 5, page 41, part of the suspicion came with how the UN dealt with the Serbs that were in UN Sector South camp after August the 4th, 1995. Isn't that so? And you noted: "I don't understand." Let's explore the Serbs that came into the camp on the night of the 4th, and let turn to your statement, if I may. And that would be at page 4 of P546 and the fourth full paragraph down you note: "A large number of displaced people were gathering outside the camp, our camp. They were asking for UN protection. These people were either civilians or children. There were no people of military service age." If we could scroll down to the bottom of that page. "Late on the evening of the 4th August 1995, we started to let the displaced people into the UN camp. Each person was searched for weapons and their personal details recorded. No Serb soldiers were allowed to enter the camp." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now that last statement "no Serb soldiers were allowed to enter the camp," that is not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn to -- if we can put 1D36-0001 on the screen. And this is an interview you did for Esprit De Corps entitled One Soldier's Story. If we could go to the first page of that. And then turn to the second page. And if we could just scroll up a bit. The other way, please. That's fine, right there. You note, and this is then talking about the people coming into the camp: "Yes, there were civilians and some military. Because we opened up the camp to displaced people to provide security, there were a few Serb soldiers that came to try to get refuge within our camp. So we said to them, 'If you want to come in, have you to disarm because if we let you in with your weapons we're putting ourselves at risk.' "So the condition was that if you want to come in, disarm yourself and you will be like everybody else. Some Serbs refused to disarm themselves so they stuck around outside the camp and those are some of the guys that were killed by a mortar round outside the camp." So, Colonel, you in fact did allow Serb soldiers into the camp, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: When you say "I," you mean the UN, not me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to your statement. In your statement - not the interview - in your statement of P546, where you say "no Serb soldiers were allowed to enter the camp," that is not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: My statement referred to the initial time when we let the people into the camp. When we first opened the gate, no Serb soldiers were allowed into the camp. That changed sometime during the night of -- of the 5th or the 6th without my knowledge at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So how many Serb soldiers were allowed into the camp?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you do know that on the 5th -- by the way, were you present when these people were searched coming in?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, did you have conversations with Captain Berikoff about what they found on these people?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No. Because, for me, General Forand gave me the task to get the camp organised. My main task was to set up a compound to hold the displaced people and organise them. So I had my Slovak engineers building the compound, getting accommodation sorted out. I believe the military police were looking after security. The civilian administrator and the staff were looking to feed the people, so there was a lot of activities going on and I couldn't be everywhere and look everywhere. I had appointed two people -- two Serb, two -- one elderly gentleman and a lady as to the point of contact between the Serb and the UN, if we had any information to pass, I would pass that information to them and if they had any requests, those were the only two that were talking to me. So I was running all over the place and was pretty hard for me to keep track of who was at the gate, who was coming in or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, going back to your interview, going back to your interview where you said that Serb soldiers disarmed, how many disarmed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't know. That -- that information would have been the discussion way after it happened with either Captain Hill, because we were neighbour at one time recollecting and talking about wartime in -- in Croatia, and I wouldn't know how many but somebody was keeping the records of all the name of the people coming in and the details, so I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So who told that you Serb soldiers had been allowed into the camp?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, is there some reason why you didn't you include this information in the witness statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Probably because I didn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if we may, if I can address our attention to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, by the way, Your Honour, I do apologise for not tendering this article. If I can just offer at this time 1D36-0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could you tell us what the date is of this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I know it is it from the magazine called Esprit de Corps, Your Honour, and I will have to go back to the hard copy and find it. Mr. Misetic is much more adept at moving through this than I, and he says he can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bellerose, I'm asking this, do you remember when you gave that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably two years ago, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because your last answer was that you left it out of your statement, that's the statement given in 1999, because you might have forgotten it, but apparently then in 2006 you still required what happened. That comes as a bit of a surprise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
