utterances.text: Your Honour, just after that -- after that statement in 1999, Captain Hill and myself were neighbour for a period of -- and we might have had some discussion and maybe talking about it, you know, about what happened in Knin or whatever, just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When Mr. Kehoe said to you that -- that no Serb soldiers were admitted into camp, that that was not true, then you said -- I think you said maybe, or something. Let me just check. You said I think I'm not sure. "I'm not sure," you said. You were sure at that time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But now, what was said in that interview, are you sure about that or are you -- I'm just trying to find out --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me, Your Honour, I don't remember seeing soldiers into the camp. By soldiers I mean people wearing combat clothing, okay? I just -- or person of fighting age. At first, there was 400 displaced people at the gate. I believe by the time they all left, there was over a thousand. I was very busy, was all over the place. I don't remember. From the interview, could have been from hearsay with talking with Captain Hill, you know, him saying that or remembering something, but to be absolutely sure that I never saw, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask the following. Don't you think that it would be have been appropriate when questions were asked about this to say, Well, whatever I said in my statement, I later learned that they were admitted, although it is hearsay information and it is not my personal observation. That would be the most complete answer which I would have expected under those circumstances. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us continue on if I can bring up P55.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way Judge, Mr. Misetic just informed me of the date of that magazine article, which was August 1, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 1 August 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think you were tendering it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- when I intervened. And there were no objections, Mr. Russo. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D513.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D513 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought the diary was D513.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. This becomes D514.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Russo. D514, being the publication in the, what was it called, the corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Esprit De Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Esprit De Corps, yes, is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could bring up P55.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a witness statement, Colonel, of a nurse at the hospital, gave testimony for the Prosecution in this case. If we can turn to the second page, paragraph 2, last sentence. If we can blow that up just a bit, centre of the page. Last two sentences. She's talking about the 5th: "There were 35 patients left behind in the hospital because they were not in a state where they could have gotten on a bus or the trucks. Most of these 35 were soldiers that had been wounded on the previous day." If we can go down to paragraph 4: "We arrived at the UN camp and told the translator that we needed to evacuate the seriously wounded. Five minutes later, three UN vehicles came with us. The UN vehicles were following our ambulance because they were worried about being shot at by RSK soldiers. The UN vehicles picked up 15 of the wounded and we took them to the UN camp. They came back and took 15 more seriously wounded." Now, Colonel, in addition to the soldiers that came in the night of the 4th into the 5th, the UN brought ARSK soldiers into the compound that you had set up inside the camp, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of us sending ambulance to pick up wounded soldier from the hospital and bring them in. That's first time I hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, is it your testimony, Colonel, that you knew nothing about wounded soldiers being brought into the UN Sector South camp? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, do you recall that UN Sector South ultimately turned over 38 individuals suspected of war crimes to the Republic of Croatia? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to clarify one answer that you gave that Mr. Misetic noted. You said that you didn't remember the UN sending ambulances to pick up -- and I'm talking about line 14: "I'm not aware of us sending ambulance to pick up wounded soldiers from the hospital and bring them in. That's the first time I hear about that."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware of the UN sending APCs to pick up wounded soldiers from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No. The only APC that I remember going there is was -- was on the 4th was I went over there with two APC, one M-113, one OT-64 to deliver medical supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, one last question on this subject. Do you know of anyone from the UN that went to the hospital to pick up anybody on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note in your statement, and we're talking about the water issues that was addressed on direct examination, and you noted for us that the water-pumping station had been hit by shell fire.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I didn't mention that it was being hit by shell, the pumping, I didn't say that. I said some of the lines seem to have been damaged on the ground because of shelling and that had been reported to me by some UN engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you got there, you did manage to restore the water, didn't you, the water flow?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when this was going on, sir, was there a public debate about the difficult circumstances under which UN Sector South found itself and that situations like water or having water on the base were quite desperate? And I refer you to page 5, paragraph 1, 2, 3, 4, first full line. Do you see that: "The Croats kept us in the camp for a considerable time."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. "The Croats kept us in the UN camp for some considerable time. We started to run out of water and things were quite desperate." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is approximately the 9th of August?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who is Major Balfour?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Major Balfour was one of the staff officer in the headquarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I know of him, not very well, but I know -- I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you D333.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could blow up this -- or just take a look at this just generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is an UN Sector South from HQ Sector South and goes to the National Defence headquarters of Canada -- to Canada dated 9 August 1995, the day you left the camp. If I can go to bottom of this at 1800 in the third sentence. "I suspect that UNPF sitreps may exaggerate the situation -- " let me back up there. "Extra page will answer your water/food question. I suspect that UNPF sitreps may exaggerate the situation for political/diplomatic effect. No real problem here with drinking water or food, even feeding 700 plus refugees." Now, Colonel, during this time was UN Sector South publicly complaining about the Croatians keeping UN in their camp with water running out when in fact water was not running out and was being exaggerated for political and diplomatic effect?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, water was a problem. And if we look at the sitrep from Mr. Major Balfour, it also say domestic water was a concern and may become a crisis if power is not restored to Knin. I don't believe that we were crying wolf, saying that we had a problem when we didn't. Because from what I recall from my time in Croatia, usually our supply used to come on Friday. The offensive started on Friday and we didn't get our resupply then. So we -- as far as I'm concerned we never got the resupply for that week, so we were continuing to feed our own people and people from the refugees with very little food that we had. Yes, the UNHCR opened up their stores so we could get flour so with that flour we were able to make some bread. But as far as I'm concerned we were having a problem with water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, what was major Balfour's position at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What's his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Formal position, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: His formal position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought he was asking for an opinion or impression about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no, no. I apologise. Wasn't a clear question, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was his position in UN Sector South?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Major Balfour was a staff officer in the headquarters. I believe he worked for -- at the time he was a captain, I believe he worked for Major Dussault, the operation officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this point he is a major; do you see?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I guess he is, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that Balfour was working for General Forand at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: He was either working for General Forand or For Major Dussault, it was one of the two. I don't fully recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just have one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I want to move back, Colonel, to the period of time that just prior to Operation Storm and you mentioned previously in your diary about the general mobilisation that had taken place on the 28th. And, if I may, turning back to your diary, if I can get the correct exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is that number? If I can call it up by the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It's D513.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in your diary you note that -- and this is at -- for July 28th. It would be page 05354629. 4620, excuse me. If we can just go back one page. Now, Colonel, this is the 28th, if we can scroll up that bottom 28th entry, this is the day that we referred to previously, the 28th, where you note that the fall of Grahovo had taken place and that general mobilisation had likewise taken place. And let us turn to the next page, at the top. Also on the 28th -- Can we scroll that down. Okay. You note that the locals are leaving the area. Now, Colonel, were you aware that on the 28th of July the president of the Krajina Serb, Milan Martic had declared a state of war?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with this, he said: "Locals are leaving the area." And if we can turn down to the next item on the 29th you note again: "The people in Knin are nervous. A lot of them are leaving town, and refugees from Bosansko Grahovo are arriving." Tell me how you came to learn that the locals were leaving town.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: That could have been one from one of the staff meeting in the morning that the information would have been passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you know of it yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Not that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me turn your attention to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can just go into private session, Judge, because this is a closed session witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just for the record, Judge, I think that anything talking about that particular exhibit that we can -- on -- I can go back and take a look at the transcript, Your Honour, and tell you when we can go back into open session, because I think -- I don't think I alerted Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is -- to change from private session to open session is a rather difficult exercise, but so therefore let's see what the importance is or whether there is any other way to make clear to the public what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But for the record I could go back to the transcript and say what questions need not be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, in your statement on page 3, paragraph 3, actually the second full paragraph, you note that you spoke to Colonel Leslie and Major Mark Dussault at 2300 hours on the 3rd of August and they told you that something was going to happen the next day. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the conclusion of the individuals there was that the war was going to start the following day. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you tell me what steps Colonel Leslie took after he received this information to alert all UN personnel that war was going to commence the next morning?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't remember any step that he took.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, at that time, did he -- you recall him sending APCs out, like he ordered you the next day to pick up UN personnel that were in the town?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't remember that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you don't remember him doing anything?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No. What I remember is him and Major Dussault were talking. I stood by, said -- you know, we talked a little bit, said something might happen tomorrow. They're not sure, and I said, well, I will keep my ears open and I went to my -- to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever ask Colonel Leslie after the fact why he didn't -- didn't call in a code red and bring everybody back in as soon as he got that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to the trip you took into Knin on the 4th. And this would be, according to your statement P545, between 1600 and 1800 hours. And if we may, if we could pull up P62, I believe it is, which should be a blank overhead of Knin. While we're bringing up this up, Colonel, the reason why you couldn't go out earlier was because the Serbs had mined the front of the camp. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you also say during the course of your statement - I believe it is it on page 4 - that a Russian officer, and I think it is the bottom of page 3, last paragraph, that one of the Russian members of UNMO left the camp with someone else and walked into Knin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in the middle of the shelling this UNMO walks into Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where did he go?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe he went to the Serb headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did he walk back?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I wasn't there when he came back. I just saw him leaving, walking. I don't remember how he came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just turning our attention to P62, which is an overhead of Knin, and just take a second to orient yourself. I mean, it is the same map as you drew on previously in P547. But if we can and with the assistance of the usher, could you map for us, Colonel, the path that you followed and I believe our colour is blue, isn't it. I believe we're using a blue marker. Could you map for us the path that you took that time between 1600 and 1800 on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: That's to go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you actually -- didn't you say you stopped at the RSK HQ, dropped off General Forand and then went on to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct. I cannot map the path, because I was inside the APC, okay? I wasn't the guy in the cupola directing the driver where to go. So was inside the vehicle. But I remember some of the area where we did stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you can't tell us based -- were you down in the APC the entire time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So what was on that road as you were travelling, you didn't see?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I didn't see it. What I saw is when we were stopped and that's when I got out of the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the hospital, and we are looking at page 4 of paragraph 4, and that would be the first paragraph -- not the carry-over paragraph on 4, it would be the first full paragraph, you observe Serb soldiers in uniform, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Injured, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Injured.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You concluded that they were Serb soldiers is the point.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yeah. Because I believe that's because they might be wearing some fatigues, uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, likewise, later on in the day when you saw people that were dead on the street, you saw people that were in uniform and I think you responded to Judge Orie that you concluded that they were soldiers as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note in this -- in your statement that, if I may, and I'm just -- that you note that it looked as if the hospital had been damaged, looked as if one corner of the hospital had been hit by a shell, it was damaged. Was it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: From what I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever learn any information from any other member of the UN that the -- that UN -- excuse me, that the hospital in Knin had been hit by a shell, anyone?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note, and I'm just going through your statement, again, on page 4 and this is the second full paragraph: "Driving through Knin on this mission, I saw a great deal of devastation." Now, use P62 that is on the screen, sir, and tell us where you saw this great devastation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could use the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's mark the first one A and the second one B, all right, and C.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's start with A. What were you doing in the area marked A?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe we were trying to get civilian UN personnel and UN police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't remember the names. Just one that I remember, it's one former Canadian -- well, a RCMP, Norm Boucher, but I don't remember exactly where he lived, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you don't know if Mr. Boucher lived in the area marked as A?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Or it could be B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Or B.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Or B. It just -- I don't exactly remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In relation to A do you know where the police station is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know where the Sanjak barracks is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: What is the Sanjak? Is that what we refer to as the north barrack?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: North barracks -- well, you can identify it. Can you see where the north barracks is? It's got a tag on it.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know where the Sanjak barracks is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who were you travelling with in the APC when you went to pick these people up?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: There was lieutenant, Jordanian that was living the M-113. I don't remember his name. He is the one that had the street address and the OT-64 was driven by Slovak or Czech soldiers that were following the 113.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Colonel, can you give us the name of anybody that was in either of these APCs that you were travelling in?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention back to A. Is that a location where you saw dead soldiers in uniform or people in uniform along with others?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe in A and B, in both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So there were soldiers in both A and B when you observed this -- these people dead. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you aware of the military facilities that were located around B?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's turn our attention to C. Did you see dead soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know the circumstances under which these people died?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I didn't go and investigate why. It was just getting out of the APC while some of the people were with me going to the building and I was just looking around and making sure that we were safe and I didn't go close to them or investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Suffice it so say, you have no knowledge as to the circumstances under which any of these people died, be it people in uniform or not in uniform, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us talk about the military targets that you talked about in both of your statement and direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, I'll offer into evidence this -- this chart that is on the screen with the blue writing on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D515.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D515 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, let's talk a bit about the shelling on the 5th and 4th if we may and then first when the shelling began at 5.00 on the 4th, you went down to a bunker, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the shelling that you observed was from the balcony from UN Sector South headquarters. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you went up to that balcony on one occasion, on the 4th, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Maybe once or twice. I cannot recall for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me turn your attention to your statement. At page 3, P546, third full paragraph after the carry-over paragraph, the paragraph beginning: "At about 0500 ... "

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can bring that up. If we can go to the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you see that, Colonel? At one time that day Captain Gilbert --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- was observing where the shells were landing, this was from the top floor of the headquarters. Before I ask the next question, Colonel, did captain Gilbert tell you about observing and chronicling outgoing fire on the 4th? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't remember. I just remember that he had a pen and a piece of paper and I think he was recording some shellings. But I don't remember him telling me outgoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But he was writing it down when you were up there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: He was writing, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, note "I joined him one time." See that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe it says "I joined him at one time."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were up with Captain Gilbert one time for 15 minutes. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Probably with Captain Gilbert one time, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who were you with any other time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe that there was one time there was a Kathy Langham might have been there one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe her name is Kathy Langham. She was one of the UN civilian employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: She was up there with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe at one time, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what time of day was this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I mean, it has been 13 years. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the rest of time you were in the bunker. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When did you get out of the bunker?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I got out of bunker about -- I was in the bunker probably about an hour, hour and a half, and -- the bunk that I was in that was basically a sea container and with sandbag on the side and on the top and after being there, for about an hour, hour and a half I decided maybe I should go to headquarters where everybody was, so I ran outside and went to the headquarters to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if that means anything, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I can tell you, for these who are not aware, the testing of the civilian warning system takes place the first Monday of every month at 12.00 exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will set my watch by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us turn our attention to P547 first, and that is your -- the chart put in by the Prosecution. If we can orient that. Looking at point A, the Prosecution, in its summation, said you observed the shelling going into point A while you were on the balcony. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to P545. Prosecution 545. Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, this is your first statement of November 1st, 1, November 1995. You wrote this, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you note at point A there were three rounds on the hill east of Knin. What hill are you talking about? And if we can, we can go back to P547. If we can flip back to P547.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: That's the one that, on a previous -- that was identified as area A, on the east side of the hill and not where there was meant -- English is my second language. What was meant was on the east side of the hill in Knin grid, so ... that's basically area A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the area A -- so you saw it falling on the hill. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let us turn your attention first to D102. If we can orient that. If I may, just orient you just for your moment, Colonel, the parliament building is 7 at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we will show you a photograph in a second to orient you yet further. Are you familiar with these various locations that are in the area of the parliament building? And I'm talking about 1 through 12, and just look through them, if you will. I don't think there is any need to read them.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Let us turn our attention to D36-0004. Now, this is the vantage point from the balcony at the UN headquarters, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No. That looked more like from the first floor than the top floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But it is from the vantage point of the UN, where UN Sector South is. You see the orientation point in the middle, the marking point of the RSK parliament. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now you the shelling that you observed that you put as point A on the hill when you noted in your statement that it was on the hill the east of Knin, or the hill at the east side of Knin, would that be in the area that is to -- well, you tell us. I mean, what area are you talking about? Is it to the left of this line where the hill goes up?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if we're going to refer to the line, can we just refer to which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The left line, the left dotted line, but I want him to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be roughly left of that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So if it is left of the line it is in fact up on the hill itself, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: It is it hard to say from that picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, whether it is up the hill depends on what you take as your point of reference, it is further up or further down, if you're talking about the top, also depending on where exactly the witness observed what he observed. So, therefore, on the hill, not on the hill is not very precise and doesn't assist greatly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Let us go down to the next chart, if I may, 1D36-0005.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, the firing that was going on, using as again your reference point down at the UN and with these other locations, it's a fact, sir, when you saw shelling going into the area you designate as A, you don't know what they were firing at, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you don't know what they hit?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So for all you know, these areas circled here on this chart, 1D36-0005, could have been the locations that were hit when you observed fire coming in on the morning of the 4th, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could put up finally 1D36-000 -- 0036 excuse me. 1D36-0006

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, again, looking at this chart, again, at the bottom of the page is the -- where the UN camp is. You gave us a grid reference at the top of grid reference 970790. Now is that also a location that you observed being shelled from the balcony at the UN?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you have any idea what was actually hit when that shelling took place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I will offer into evidence 1D36-0004, 1D36-0005 1D36-0006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these become Exhibit D516 through D518, respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn our attention to D131. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it assist you to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D516 through D518 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I apologise for getting ahead of myself there. Can I do D131?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as we bring this up, Colonel, let me reference you back to your direct testimony as well your statement, you say, in my opinion, the shelling of Knin was carried out -- this is on page 7, I apologise, the second-to-last paragraph. Page 7 of P546. You say that: "In my opinion, the shelling of Knin was carried out to drive away the civilian population. The shelling was not directed at any military targets." Now, let's take that one by one if we can as quickly as we can. I want to take a look at it this first chart that's designated and encircled. The first location, sir, is A-1, the northern barracks, that's what you talked about, right, as a target?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yeah, if that is the northern barracks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can zoom in there if you want, but orient yourself with the UN building at the bottom. Do you see that as the northern barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the B-1 at the bottom, that's the ARSK headquarters, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go to the next chart. Now, we've added what is added for you slide by slide has a plus mark in front of it. Do you see the parliament building at B-8. You're familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how about B-10, the police station. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, C-3 was an artillery position behind your camp. You know about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you didn't know there was an artillery position behind your camp?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, how about the factory, the Agroprerada, excuse me, Agroprerada depot at D-2, were you aware of that near the train station?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And of course, you know that you have E-6 which is the train station management wagons tracks? Do you see that? You were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next layer, talking about ARSK troop bases and barracks. No, it's the next -- it was the slide back. If we can go ahead one. Okay. Looking at the blue box on the left-hand side, Colonel, we mentioned the northern barracks is A-1. A-2 is the Senjak barracks. Are you familiar with the Senjak barracks being run by the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about A-3, the southern barracks, that was next to you, you were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And A-4, which was the high school, are you aware of a Serb military unit being garrisoned at A-4 and that they had a mortar emplacement there on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let go to A-5, which is the ARSK special police. Are you aware of that location?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next slide. This would be dealing with RSK command and control and power. Let's talk about the lower left green box. We talked previously about B-1, the ARSK HQ. Let's talk about B-2, ARSK -- which is part of the defence ministry, it's known as the old hospital. Were you aware that was being used by the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: B-3 again, the same item called the seniors hotel, were you aware that was being used by the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about B -- just read it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be better solution if you would give the witness the list of all what you consider to be military targets and to ask him simple questions after the break, one of them, first of all, were you aware of the presence of the facilities described there; second, if you were aware of them, is there any reason why you did not consider them to be potential military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do that quickly, Judge, I can go to the last side which has all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we're still reading half in green but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can go to the last slide, which has all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go to -- if we can go I guess three slides into -- one prior to that. That one. It is it 0396, I'm being told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the full list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's the full list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Give that to the witness and I mean it may be clear to him now what the questions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just give him a moment just to review the entire list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we could also do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- for me, the time I was there, the only one I was aware of was the south barracks, the ARSK headquarters downtown Knin, and the northern barracks. Everything else, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you did not consider any of the others as to their existence or to their potential as a military target when you formed your opinion about that there was no -- it wasn't where military targets were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the existence of those other -- other location0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just moving ahead, are you familiar with the concept, Colonel, of mobile targets?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what are mobile targets, what is your understanding of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Well, it's -- let's say a piece of equipment, like tracked artillery that one minute it is in one location, fire a couple of rounds, and then redeploy to a different location. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And -- yes, sir. And then likewise would include soldiers on foot as well, being moving through an area. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us just briefly touch on that in D124. D124 is a situation report of 5 August 1995. And if we could go to the bottom of that page first. Now just as a reference point there, it notes at the bottom that Serbs towns, Benkovac, Gracac, Vrlika, Drnis are taken by HV forces, early in the morning Serbs started massive withdrawal of combat forces from the general area Benkovac and Kistanje towards the general direction of Knin. If we could just move up two more pages. One more page, please, and towards the bottom is the CanBat, Canadian Battalion AOR. We don't need to read that but if you can take a look at it, Colonel, and ... What CanBat reports is a significant amount of military equipment from the ARSK moving towards the general direction of Knin. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just turn over to the next page, just quickly. Likewise, more equipment moving towards Knin and if you look towards the top you see where it is headed towards Knin. Now, Colonel, those particular pieces, do you know if they moved through Knin at any time during the 4th or the 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if they did, they certainly would be movable targets that were open for shelling by the HV, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, if he is going to ask the witness what is appropriate to shell, then we would certainly like to investigate that on redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm asking if it is a movable target and if it's going through the Knin on the 4th or 5th, if the HV could shell it. Given what the counsel asked on direct examination, I don't see anything improper in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting it is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is not that easy, Mr. Kehoe. You know that, of course, it very much depends on where they were driving, what kind of weaponry was used, et cetera. So if you would say whether -- apart from that, it is based on the assumption, if they were there, could they have been shelled or I would prefer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- being attacked. I take it that moving troops in itself, whatever the witness would say, if they are taking active part in operations, that there's a great likelihood that they are legitimate military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the difficult part starts. Yes? Who they were, where they were, what other issues issue, et cetera, so I take it that the witness would not disagree with what I just said, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- I would not disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's why we have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interesting thing is how do you know where they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because that's the assumption in the question, and of course, you would have to establish that to answer some of the follow-up questions. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you note the during the course of your direct examination, and pardon me if I misquote this but I trust I will get the general idea, that one of the reasons that you thought that this shelling was intended to drive out the civilian population is because military targets weren't seriously damaged by the artillery attack? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to D389. This is a document from the RSK headquarters from the 4th of August, 1995, and it discusses the shelling commencing on 4 August 1995. And if we can look at the fourth paragraph down Knin was attacked by Livansko Polje. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. It's the middle of the page. It says Knin was attacked --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Okay, yes, I do, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just read that with me, Knin was attacked -- and by the way, just to reference you again, Colonel, this is an ARSK document. Knin was attacked from the Livansko polje from different directions and by the time this information was drafted between 200 and 300 rounds of different calibre impacted on the town. The first strike was carried out on the building of the SVK General Staff which suffered great materiel damage with the fleet of vehicles almost completely deployed. Later the fire was transferred on the military barracks, 1300, Kaplara, the Tvik factory, railway intersection, residential buildings and the area beneath the Knin fortress, the item that we looked at previously in D102. Were you aware, sir, that the initial barrage of fire had in fact damaged these particular locations, the SVK General Staff the vehicles, military barracks, Tvik factory, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me, can if I will, and Your Honour, if I can just go into private session, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If can I take a break right now -- I will do either one, Judge, whatever you want to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that would be the better solution, because I take it that have you to ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have to ask a couple of questions about testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and since it is 12.30, we'd prefer to have a break first. We will have a break and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a provisional assessment done by the UNMOs and if we look down at paragraph 2 it notes: "In general the shelling was concentrated against military objectives. The damages caused by shelling to civilian establishments is concentrated to the close vicinity of military objectives. Only few, three to five, impacts is observed in other urban areas." Were you aware of this assessment, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted during the course of your testimony -- excuse me. And this would be, I should not your testimony, I should say your statement, P546, page 6, bottom of the page, starting with the paragraph: "I did not notice." Just the last paragraph, yeah, that's it. "Brigadier-general Forand tasked CIVPOL with preparing a report on the damage that had been caused throughout Sector South." Do you see that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see the results of that report?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you ever informed that the results of that report were consistent with the provisional assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also noted for us during the course of your testimony that the shelling constituted deliberate harassment not only on the 4th but that the 5th was -- shelling on the 5th was unnecessary. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the fighting still continued between the RSK and the HV through the evening of the 4th, into the 5th, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I cannot say if it did or did not. I was inside the compound so I mean we could hear artillery. I don't remember if we did hear small arms or not, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you D106. And this is an interview with General Mrksic and Belgrade Radio on 4 August 1995 at 2130 hours. The fourth delineation down with General Mrksic: "No. We are maintaining contact, our forces withdrew to the positions for the direct defence of Knin. The other range units are still successfully holding their positions." If we can move further down that page. Seven lines from the bottom, "if the VRS army of the Republika Srpska succeeds in putting pressure on the forces attacking in the direction Grahovo-Knin, we shall then stabilize the defense and switch on the counterattack." Let me show you one last item. Actually, I can read it. It's on the video of General Leslie. This would be from D123. There is no need to listen to the video but he notes: "At 2340 hours on the 4th, taking Knin, no, we have no reports of Croatians being in direct fire range of Knin and there are still a lot of Serbs in Knin and in the surrounding hills." So, Colonel, was it your understanding that through the evening of the 4th and going on the 5th there continued to be fighting between the RSK and the HV?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I really don't know. You got to understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have to understand that I didn't go too often in the command centre of HQ Sector South. I was very busy, you know, doing engineer-related work inside the camp. So if reports were coming in from various sources, I wasn't aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, on the 5th -- I'm sorry. On the 5th, Colonel, did you know or did you observe RSK military returning from the front lines through Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say, Colonel, that on the 5th you were unaware of the military situation that was ongoing between the HV and the ARSK. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you mentioned going through the town of Knin on the 9th, I believe, which is where you -- and I'm talking about page 5, fourth full paragraph down, where you viewed the devastation everywhere in Knin town.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that, again, is in P546. Let me just refer to you a couple of matters, and first D29. Second paragraph. This is a cable from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan. Paragraph 2: "My overall impression of the town in Knin is that it suffered considerable damage from artillery fire which is evident in the streets where I observed many shops with broken window, cars damaged and off the road, artillery shell holes in the road. However, the damage to the town's structures, while noticeable, was less than I anticipated. Large numbers of homes and buildings were left untouched by the fighting." If I may, a witness, Mr. Flynn, a Prosecution witness who was a HRAT representative. This is on page 1156, testimony before this Court on 10 April 2008, line 7. During his visit Mr. Akashi met a number of people and also toured Knin, as you told us yesterday? "Answer: Yes." "Question: His overall impression of the town of Knin is that it suffered considerable damage from artillery fire," and he gives his observations. "However, the damage to the town structures, while noticeable, was less than I anticipated." "Would that accord -- talking to Mr. Flynn, would that accord with your observations of Knin?" "Yes." Question, he goes on to say, "Large numbers of homes and buildings were left untouched by the fighting. Would that accord with your observations?" "Answer: Yes." Ambassador Galbraith, page 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ambassador Galbraith at 24 June 2008, page 5044, line 19: "In any event so we had -- we had people there I think on the 7th and 9th of August looking at what had happened in Knin." The 9th of August is was when you went down there, right, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Looking at what had happened, and all of them reported to me that the damage from the shelling was not extensive, in fact that things were largely undamaged and that windows were broken, that sort of thing had happened and there was no -- there was no kind of systematic effort to destroy Knin." Lastly, if we can turn our attention to D66, and after we go through these, I'll ask you a question, Colonel. Going to the bottom of that page, this is a US cable dated 14 August 1995, notes at downtown Knin: "Although Knin was reportedly heavily shelled in the early hours of the hostilities few downtown areas and residential buildings showed signs of shell damage." As you sit here, Colonel, is it that you disagree with all these other individuals who made these observations during the same time-frame when you were in Knin after the end of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I do not disagree. What I would like to say is that I never really counted all the building and it's just like if somebody is to assess the stress level on an individual, we will be looking at the stress at the different level, you know, so certain situation, you might find very stressful and I might not, or the other way around. I don't know what they use as a reference. But for me, I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, had you ever been in combat before prior to this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us change our focus for one moment to talking about the looting that you talked about in your statement. And that would again be on page 5. Colonel, you mentioned looting and the clothing being thrown out. Did you personally see a looting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the law enforcement or soldiers that were searching these places were looking for weapons, and, if so, did they find any?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you don't know the circumstances of the looting that you talked about in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No. Well, for me in my statement I was referring to that people had been going through various buildings or most of the building, clothing, furniture had been thrown out of the window and not knowing what was there prior, I just assumed that it was looting had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You assumed that, but you didn't know if it was a search for weapons or anything else?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And going through a city and any type of fighting in the built-up area, you would expect soldiers to search apartments looking for weapons, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the last topic we had to talk about is the topic that you referred to with regard to the soldier that you examined up -- by one of the observation posts and you mention it on page 5. This is on the 12th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, mentioned to us on direct examination that have you no forensic background; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what you observed was a RSK soldier lying flat on the ground with a gunshot wound to his sternum; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not to his head to his sternum?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe it was the sternum, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that during the course of any combat that was going on, if individuals took that body from one location and laid it out so it could be found and be buried?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So that is equally plausible as to any explanation or any hypothesis you might come up with; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It went much more quickly than I thought, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was noticed by the interpreters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can ask a few more questions, Judge. That was a joke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I always admire them to be able to follow. Then Mr. Kuzmanovic, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Bellerose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bellerose, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic who is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the registrar please pull up D513. The last four digits of the page number are 4620; that's the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the diary that you produced here that we received a copy of goes through Sunday, July 30, or actually Monday, July 31. Did you have any other entries beyond Monday, July 31?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You stopped keeping the diary after the end of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the document up on the screen, point number 4 under Saturday, July 29 -- 29 July, it says: "Murray Dawes is trying to get Jordana, his interpreter/secretary, out"? What did you mean by that entry?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe that I meant that he was trying to get her out of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was on the 29th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: It would appear so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he relate to you why he was trying to get her out of Knin on July 29th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, were the interpreters that you hired of Serb ethnicity at the camp?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I believe they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to your statement, the November 1999 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could pull that up, please. And if we go to page 6, the top of page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you have that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just for your own reference if you go to the page before, at the very bottom it says on 12 August 1995, you went to Serb observation post that was close to either CanBat, et cetera. Then the next page -- I'm assuming that what you are talking about on the next page where you say: "Once we were allowed to leave the UN camp," that all happened after August 12th of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No. That would have been on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you get the order from General Forand to start dismantling the observation posts, what date?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure exactly, but that would have been the week following the offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So around the 12th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Probably, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So from August 12th on, you were -- your job was to start dismantling all of your observation posts?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That meaning the UN observation posts?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, how many of these observation posts were there, roughly?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: About 120 that I recall. That's in the four sector -- I mean four section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That was -- what area are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: The Kenyan area sector of operation, the Canadians, the Jordanian, and the Czech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it was in Sector South and partly in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, just Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the Czech observation post located?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: In the northern part of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know where exactly?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: If I had a map showing the border between Sector North and Sector South, I could show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's refer you then, I guess back to your statement here, on page 6. You said that you -- you had orders to dismantle all your observation posts. Did you have a time-frame within which you had to accomplish that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where you -- where you started?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Well, there was concurrent activity. Every battalion, like the Kenyans and the Canadian and the Jordanian and the Czech, were starting dismantling at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just give me a moment here, Your Honour. I'm trying to find a map. Call up P307, please. And if we could enlarge that, please. If we could scroll down a little bit please. Right, that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you see where Knin is circled there on this particular map?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for me -- if could you use a pointer just for demonstrative purpose, where the observation posts in general were located? Not all 120 obviously, but general locations of where the observation posts were?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: You don't have a map that shows the former borders between the Krajinas and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We probably do, but if you -- for sake of simplicity if you could just show us, for example, I guess, can you tell me where is JorBat located on this map?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I remember the Kenyan in this sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you have marked a half circle in blue?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yeah, that is K for Kenyan. Roughly, we had the Canadian. I believe JorBat were along the mountain. And further up we had the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You can't scroll up anymore now that you have drawn on it but further north would be the Czechs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Would be the Czech, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- mark with that exactly where the JorBat location was there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: There's not enough detail nor I do remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what city it was located in? If you don't know, you can tell me you don't know.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, back to your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D519 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 1999 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go back to that, Mr. Registrar, on page 6. Just that first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Toward the middle of that paragraph you talk about restriction of movement in the sector and you state: "I saw Croatian special police at the entrance to many villages. They would often refuse us entry to these villages." First of all, from whom did you get that information? What factual basis do have you to state that they were Croatian special police?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly how I was told that those people in -- that type of uniform were special police, but for me the normal police were wearing dark blue and a force cap and usually just have a side-arm and driving the green and white vehicle. The soldiers were usually wearing fatigue uniform with camouflage pattern and those persons stopping us, I call them the special police, were wearing a one colour uniform, either very dark grey or black and had load bearing vests and looked a lot more professional than normal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd specifically asked you -- thank you for that answer, but I'd specifically asked you what factual basis did you have to say in your statement that they were Croatian special police?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Other than the uniform they were wearing and assuming that based on the uniform they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell what kind of -- you said that they had a cap, a certain kind of cap. What kind of cap did they have?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, the normal police were wearing -- I call that a force cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Like a normal street cop would have?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Like a normal street cop would have. But those that I call the special police didn't wear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did have any kind of thing -- hat or cap on their head?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: It has been 18 years I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed that in the statement that gave in 1999 you did not mention anything about the colour of the uniforms or what kind of vests that they had. Yet we have a supplemental statement here from you that was given on 30th June that discusses in some detail what kind of uniforms these gentlemen were wearing. Can you describe why all of a sudden on June 30th of 1998 you recall that kind of detail?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Probably the question wasn't asked in 1999 how I can make the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You also didn't mention specifically any towns or villages that you claim the special police refused entry to you in back 1999; yet specifically in your supplemental statement given on June 30th, 1998, you recall one of those times happening in the area of Gracac. What has given you the clarity to now remember Gracac?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Just that I recall that area, because going into the south, in the Kenyans' sector of operation, I don't recall ever being stopped in that area. But going towards the north I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So you assumed it was Gracac or you think it was Gracac, or is it a guess?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that was near Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the dates were?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many times you were -- you claim you were refused entry into villages?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I cannot be specific. Maybe, two, three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How many people were at these spots in which you claim you were prevented from entering villages?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
