utterances.text: How many people were with you on these trips?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Probably me and a Slovak driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No. And I had different driver every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it was you and a driver and the drivers you can't remember who they are?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of vehicle did you have?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I had a Toyota pick-up truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What colour?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: White.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if you can, did you ever have any conversations with those people at these spots where you said that you were prevented from entering?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Yeah. I cannot remember exactly what was said, but they wouldn't let me in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you say, what did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I probably would have told them that I was a UN and I was going to one of the UN observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the reply?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would they speak English to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Some did. Very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were on your way to observation posts, how did you get there? Were you using the main roads?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Some were main roads; some were tracks that had been build by the UN to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: To get to those spots?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: To get to the those spots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were those dirt roads, then?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Some were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So just so I'm straight, you can't give me a date or dates when you were stopped, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you can't give me the locations other than the general area of Gracac of places that you were stopped. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you can't give me the name of anybody you were with when you were stopped. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, can you give me a date of when you went -- when you were stopped in and around the area of Gracac? And I'm sorry if I asked that already.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell of the kind of insignia that any of these people who stopped you wore?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have insignia?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, again, you cannot tell me what factual basis you came to conclude that these people who stopped you were actually Croatian special police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: I was assuming by their uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the special police was organised or structured?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the military police was organised or structured?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the Croatian military was organised or structured?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Nothing arises. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing arises. Mr. Russo, any need re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Referring back to your statement, P546, page 3, last paragraph, you mentioned that "I was unable to leave Sector South immediately to carry out these tasks. This was because Serbs had put a number of surface mines on the road was directly outside of the camp gates and leading up to the main road." Could you please clarify this issue, was it -- when it occurs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: That was on the 4th, after -- well, now General Leslie asked me to go and deliver the medical supply. We got the APC organised, the medical loaded and when we got at the gate there was Serb soldiers stopping us from leaving and they also had a mine on the surface of the road, so, you know, preventing us from leaving with our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But did they allow to you they mine this area or they prohibit to do it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH LORENZO CLAUDE BELLEROSE
utterances.text: Well, they didn't have to say that they mined the area. We could see that the mine were on the road, that the mine were, let's say, less than five metres from the main gate. And they weren't buried; they were right on the surface of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I have no further questions for you, Mr. Bellerose, this concludes your testimony, unless the question by Judge Kinis has triggered any need to put further questions to the witness. Mr. Bellerose, I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague. I saw in this interview that you were a bit surprised at the time that you were never called to testify. Well, that has now changed. Mr. Bellerose, I wish you a safe trip home again and thank you for answering all the questions asked by the parties and by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And sorry for a bit of confusion at the beginning. I was a bit nervous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope that's over now. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Bellerose out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We asked for only two minutes to read a decision and I got even ten. The Chamber still owes the parties the reasons for granting trial-related protective measures for Witness 3. On the 4 April 2008, the Prosecution applied for the trial-related protective measures of pseudonym and face distortion for Witness 3. On the 16th April 2008, the Gotovina Defence filed a response, in which it did not oppose the request but disagreed with the Prosecution's arguments in support of the motion. The following day, the Markac Defence filed a joinder to that response. And on the 21 April 2008 the Chamber decided to grant the request with reasons to follow. This decision can be found at transcript page 1862. After the request was granted, the Chamber was informed in private session that information about the anticipated evidence of the witness had entered the public domain. The Chamber consequently decided to hear the testimony of the witness in private session. This decision can be found at transcript page 1870. As the Chamber held in its reasons for its first protective measures decision in this case at transcript page 2610, the mere expression of fear by a person is not sufficient for protective measures to be granted. The party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. Witness 3, a Croatian Serb, travels regularly to Croatia, where she owns property. She has expressed fears of encountering certain persons whom she met during the course of events pleaded in the indictment. After careful consideration, the Chamber found that the content of her anticipated testimony could antagonise those persons. The witness has been approached and questioned by journalists, who published stories on her connection with the indictment. This further fueled her fears. For these reasons, the Chamber is satisfied that the Prosecution has demonstrated an objectively grounded risk to the security of the witness should it become known that she has given evidence before the Chamber. The Chamber considered the information about the anticipated evidence of the witness that had fallen into the public domain and found that the only effective way to protect her identity was to hear her testimony in private session. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision to grant protective measures for Witness 3. There's not sufficient time to call another witness. Nevertheless, the Chamber would briefly explore what will happen in the days to come. We have a witness scheduled for tomorrow, which will not take much time in chief, as far as I'm informed. Mr. Hedaraly, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It should take 45 minutes or an hour, at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At most. Any idea on how much cross-examination would take of the next witness to appear?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would anticipate right now, Your Honour, two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two to three hours. Other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As things stand, Your Honour, we don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that depends on cross-examination of Mr. Misetic, but I don't believe we will take more than 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that -- now I get three messages at the same time, so if you'd just give me one second. Can we move into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Registrar. As I said before, we'll resume tomorrow, the 8th of July, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II.
